title: Dreamer (Träumer) - the manual
subtitle: The whole game from the screen to the bots: every move, every card, every setting - and a guided demo game that plays the first rounds with you.

welcome.title: Welcome to Dreamer
welcome.intro: Dreamer (Träumer in German) is a money game you play on a map, with dice and cards, **inside your own books**: a salary is a real booking, a share is a real Grow project, a dream is a real Dream project. You live a character through years of money decisions - and when the game is over you know what a reserve, a loan, an index or a payment plan does, because you made them do it.

items.title: The aim
items.text: Build a life you can afford: repay what you owe, keep a reserve, **live your dream** and let your money work for you until **passive income pays your bills**. When all five goals of your character are true, you have won.

items.title: How it is played
items.text: You roll the dice, your **totem** walks a map of tiles, and every tile is a pile of cards: Opportunities to invest in, Harvest cards that move the markets, Emergencies, Life, Career, Dreams and Paydays.

items.title: Alone or together
items.text: You always play at a **table**: against bots (as many as you like) or against other people. Everybody lives their own life in parallel; the markets are shared. **The first to reach every goal wins.**

items.title: A rating
items.text: Ranked games move your **rating** (everybody starts at 1500) on one leaderboard with people and bots. Unranked games are for learning and for fun.

blocks.title: Who can read this and play
blocks.text: The game and this manual are for **game accounts** on the self-hosted edition: an account whose email contains the word `cashflow`. Nothing in such an account is real money, and nothing you do reaches a normal account.
The fastest way to understand it

Do not read this page from the top first. Start the **guided demo game**: a table against a friendly bot with a fixed die and fixed cards, where a coach shows you every place of the screen and every move in about fifteen minutes. You can stop it at any moment and play for real. You find it in four places:

items: the **Demo** button at the top right of every page of the app, while you are signed in with a game account (without an account, or with a normal one, it starts the normal demo of the Money Manager);
the **Dreamer lobby**, on the entry **Learn the game**;
**the demo bot**: when you add the bot called **Coach** to a table, the table is the demo;

blocks.text: How this manual is built

It goes from the top of the screen to the bottom of the game: **the screen**, **your money**, **your life**, **the map and a turn**, then **every card type** one by one, **selling**, **playing together**, **ratings**, **the bots**, **strategy**, a **FAQ** and a **glossary**. The last section holds the numbers of thousands of simulated games. Every section stands on its own: use the list on the left (or the menu at the top on a phone) to jump.

blocks.title: Words in this manual
blocks.text: Money is counted in **Dream Taler** (DT, in German **Traumtaler**, TT) unless the table chose a real currency sign. A **Payday** is a month: your salary comes in and your bills go out. **Fire**, **Dream**, **Grow** and **Mojo** are the places your money lives; the section "Your money" explains each.

firstgame.title: Your first game, step by step
firstgame.intro: From the lobby to the first Payday. Nothing here can go wrong: the first game is a game against a bot, and you can leave it any time.

items.title: Open the lobby
items.text: In the menu choose **Tables**, and at the top of the lobby switch from **Classic** to **Dreamer**. You see the open tables, your own tables, the leaderboard and the **Join with a code** field.

items.title: Open a table
items.text: Press the round **+**. Give the table a name (or take the suggestion), choose the **difficulty** (start on **Normal**; Easy is gentler), leave **Ranked** off for a first game, and press **Open the table**. Every setting is explained in "Playing together".

items.title: Seat a bot
items.text: In the waiting room press **Add bot**. Choose a strategy and a level, or the bot **Coach** for the guided demo. A table needs at least two seats.

items.title: Meet your character
items.text: Everybody first reads **who they are**: the story, the goals, the income, the bills and the debts. Choose your insurances (they count at once) and press **I am ready**. Until then you may go back and take another character, unless the table deals the characters.

items.title: Start and roll
items.text: When everybody is ready the host presses **Start**. On your turn press the golden **dice**. The totem walks and the card of the tile opens.

items.title: Decide, then press Done
items.text: Read the card, decide (the buttons say what each choice costs) and press **Done**. If a market card touched something you own, Done takes you to **Grow** and marks what changed.

items.title: Settle the month
items.text: Passing a **Payday** tile pays your salary and takes your bills. What is left is yours: put it into the reserve, a payment plan for the dream, or a card you planned.

items.title: Keep going until the goals are true
items.text: About **90 turns** make a normal game. You win when your reserve, your debts, your dream and your independence are all done.

blocks.title: A first Payday, in numbers
blocks.text: Jonas, the dual student, earns about 1,955 DT net and has bills for the rest; about **500 DT** are left over. He puts 100 into the reserve, plans 50 a month into his dream, and keeps the rest as cash for the next card. After a month or two his **free saving cards** (a cheaper phone plan, cheaper electricity) lift that sum without costing anything.

blocks.title: Where to look when you do not know what to do
blocks.text: The row of **goals** shows what is still missing, the **strip above the map** shows what is running on your money, and the **info of your character** lists everything again. The demo game and the section "Strategy" tell you what to do first.

screen.title: The game screen, from top to bottom
screen.intro: Everything on the screen has one job. This is the whole tour; the demo game walks you through the same places while you play.

items.title: The map
items.text: A closed track of tiles. Your **totem** stands next to the tile you are on and points at it; the other players' totems wear their initials or pictures. A tile is coloured by its kind (gold Payday, purple Opportunity, amber Harvest, green Dream, red Emergency, pink Life, blue Career).

items.title: The badges of your life
items.text: Small badges (relationship, children, home, place, job, pet, car, education, insurances, career). **Tap one** and a card tells what it means. They decide which cards can happen to you.

items.title: The strip: what is running
items.text: Above the map: every effect that works on your money right now and **how many Paydays are left** - a cost that runs for a while, a pause, a gain, a job search.

items.title: The goals
items.text: The five goals of your character as bars in percent: **debts**, **reserve**, **dream**, **independence** (and dream points where the table asks). A bar turns gold when done.

items.title: The money panel
items.text: Cash, reserve, passive income against the cost of living, monthly cash flow, net worth, the Bank loan. Put money into the reserve or the dream, repay a debt or the loan, here.

items.title: Grow, Dream and Fire
items.text: The three project pages: **Grow** (your investments), **Dream** (your dreams with their buckets) and **Fire** (what must be paid: the reserve, emergencies). The project pages are the normal pages of the Money Manager.

items.title: The balance
items.text: The income statement and the balance sheet of your character: income, expenses, assets, liabilities. Every card you take changes them.

items.title: History and feed
items.text: The feed tells what everybody does ("Anna rolls the dice", "Coach buys ..."). A line opens the card it is about. The history keeps every step; **Undo** takes back the last action of your turn.

items.title: The players
items.text: The queue of players shows who is on the move, who is a bot, who is away, and the clock. Tap a player to **look at their books** (read only) and go back with **Back to my books**.

items.title: The table menu
items.text: Settings (pop-ups and messages on or off), **pause**, **autoplay while I am away**, the table's rules, **Resign** and, in the demo, **Stop the tutorial**.

aim.title: The aim: five goals, one win
aim.intro: A game ends when somebody wins, goes bankrupt, resigns or runs out of turns. This is what "winning" means.

blocks.text: Every character has a list of goals. For Jonas, **all five must be true**:

items: Pay back the loan from your parents (1,500 TT).
Pay back the car loan (1,500 TT).
Fund and live the **dream** - every bucket of the project full.
Build the **reserve**: three monthly expenses in the Mojo.
Become **financially independent**: passive income covers all monthly expenses.

blocks.text: **The Financial independence badge** 💎 appears as soon as the passive income covers the expenses (the part of the expenses that comes from your salary - income tax and social insurance - is not counted against your passive income, because it stops when the salary stops). The game goes on: the badge is a milestone, not the end.
**When every goal is done** the **win screen** appears, with a trophy, the ticked goals and the numbers of your game; you may keep playing.
**Bankruptcy.** If the monthly cash flow turns negative the game ends.
**How long is a game?** A normal game is about **90 turns** (roughly 36 months), a fast one 30, a long one 120.

blocks.title: The honest truth about the order
blocks.text: In thousands of simulated games the reserve and the dream were reached long before the income. A player who funded the dream before there was any income has rarely won. **Income is the bottleneck.**

money.title: Your money: five accounts, Grow, plans and the Bank
money.intro: The game uses the five accounts of the Barefoot Investor method plus an investment tracker called Grow. If you know the Money Manager you know them already; if not, this section is the whole idea.

head: Account
What it is for
rows: Bills and everyday life: rent, food, insurance. Your salary lands here.
Spending that is only for fun.
Your dreams. Every dream is a **Dream project** with buckets (flights, hotel, equipment...) that you fill.
What must be paid: emergencies, the reserve, investments. Every payment to an Emergency or a purchase is a **Fire** transaction.
Your emergency reserve: three months of expenses. It is a Fire project from day one and may only be used for emergencies.

blocks.text: **Grow** is where investments live: every card you take becomes a **Grow project** (a share, an investment or an asset) with its numbers, notes and tasks. You buy and sell with the normal Buy and Sell buttons of Grow.

**Payment plans.** A big goal (the reserve, a dream bucket) is not paid at once: you set up a payment plan that moves part of every month's free money into it. The game does not force you; it shows what is due.

**The Bank loan.** If a payment is bigger than your cash, the Bank lends you the missing amount automatically. It costs **10% of the loan every month** (a setting) - a loan is an emergency tool, not a way of investing.

**Insurance.** You start with liability and household insurance. An emergency that an insurance covers costs you only the deductible; you can hop in or out of an insurance with the next Payday. Without it, the bill is yours.
Dream: your dream, with buckets

A dream is a **Dream project**. It has **buckets** (the flights, the hotel, the equipment ...) and each bucket has a price. Money goes into a bucket by hand or, much better, by a **payment plan**: "50 a month into the dream" moves 50 at every Payday until the bucket is full. A dream you have fully funded is **lived** - it pays out its dream points and ticks the dream goal.
Mojo and Fire: the reserve and what must be paid

The **Mojo** is your reserve: three months of living costs. It is a **Fire project** from the first day and may only be used for emergencies. **Fire** is the account of everything that has to be paid - an emergency, the reserve, a debt, an investment you booked.
Grow: where your investments live

Every card you take becomes a **Grow project** with its numbers, its notes, its tasks and its risk. A share has units and a price, a property has a deposit and a mortgage, a business has a monthly cash flow. In Grow you **buy** and **sell** with the normal buttons; every dice roll, sale and market effect is written into the **notes** of the project with the numbers.
Payment plans

A big goal is never paid at once. A **plan** moves part of every Payday's free money into a project: the reserve, a dream bucket, an emergency you spread over 3, 6 or 12 Paydays. The game never forces a plan; it shows what is **due**. A plan can be raised, lowered or stopped at any time (`0` stops it).
The Bank loan

If a payment is bigger than your cash the **Bank** lends you the missing amount automatically. It costs **10% of the loan every month** (a table setting). A loan is an emergency tool, not a way to invest: **repay it as soon as the cash allows**. A bot that keeps a loan open when it could repay it loses points in the simulation.

blocks.title: Why 10% a month matters
blocks.text: Nothing in the game earns 10% a month. Selling a card to repay the Bank is almost always right - the bots do it too (the capability **sell to clear a loan**).
Insurance

You start with liability and household insurance, paid at every Payday. When an insured emergency hits, you pay only the **deductible** (at most 500 DT on Normal, 300 on Easy, 750 on Hard). Before the first roll a change counts at once; later it counts from the **next Payday**, so nobody insures just before the fire. See "Your life" for the car insurances.

blocks.text: The map: characters, strategies and difficulties

The simulation has played every character, on every difficulty, with every way of playing (200 games each, same seeds): the **map**. It is what the bots of the multiplayer game are drawn from and what the analyst compares a saved game with. `docs/dreamfund-balance/MATRIX.md` has the whole table, `matrix.json` the numbers. Run `npm run matrix:dreamfund` to make it again whenever a card, a character or a number changes. The best strategy of each character and difficulty (share of games won in up to 60 months):
The Yin Yang map

A circle with an S through it (2026-11-04). Every player walks one whole side: the **white** track is the S and the left half of the circle, the **black** track the right half of the circle and the S walked the other way. The S (with its two ends, where the sides meet) is common ground - the same tiles for both tracks, and all the Paydays except one more on each side of a large map. Each track has the tiles of the size (24, 36 or 48) with the usual mix. The seats take the tracks in turn, white first; with an odd number of players one side has one more. Both start on opposite sides of the circle - each on the first tile of their own half - walk their half, and meet on the S. The two dots of the symbol show the players of each side with their pictures. Solo, the player walks the white track.

blocks.text: Where the life starts

Jonas starts as a **dual student**: a room in a **shared flat** (that is the rent line of his budget), **employed** half-time, **in education** - the study ends with his first full-time contract, at stage 2 of his career. The other nine characters start where their story says: Lena alone with her daughter, Katrin and Frank married with children, Peter married with grown children. The first table below says it for everybody.
Insurances

The insurances of a character are **expense lines**: the premium is paid at every Payday, and in return an insured emergency costs you only the **deductible** - at most 500 TT on Normal (300 on Easy, 750 on Hard), whatever the bill is. Every character starts with the private **liability** and the **household** insurance, and every character pays **its own price**: a surgeon's household is worth more than a bus driver's, a freelancer carries his own liability. Jonas pays 24 TT a month for the two together (8.39 + 15.61); the others are scaled to their life, and the last column of the first table shows what they pay.

items: **At the start** you are asked to choose: before your first roll you can hop in or out of every insurance, and it counts **at once**.
**Later** a change is made at the **next Payday** - the premium and the cover change together, so nobody can insure just before the fire.

**A car brings the car insurances.** As soon as you have a car (a vehicle dream, a company car, a card), the **partial cover** (Teilkasko) and the **full cover** (Vollkasko) are on offer in the insurance list, with a premium that fits your character. They cost nothing until you hop in; an uninsured car damage costs the whole bill.
The private **liability** also covers the lost building key. A stolen bike is not insured by anything on this list.

turn.title: A turn, from the roll to the last decision

blocks.text: At a table every player first reads **who they are**: the story, what matters to them, the goals, the income, the expenses and the debts - and chooses the **insurances**, which count at once. Until you say you are ready you can go back and choose another character (unless the characters are drawn). The game is begun in the background; the first turn starts when everybody is ready.

items: **Roll** the dice (one or two; some cards say which).
The totem walks. Passing a Payday tile pays you; landing on a tile opens its card.
Deal with the card - the cards below explain how - and press **Done** (Fertig).
If a Harvest card touched something you own, **Done** takes you to Grow, where the affected projects are marked and every effect is written into the project's notes.

blocks.text: **Every die is yours to throw.** Whenever a card is decided by a die you press the golden dice yourself. Before you throw, the card shows **what each number does**, coloured green (good), red (bad) or grey. This is true for Life cards, for Opportunity cards (the purchase waits for your throw and Done is refused until you have thrown) and for the dice of Harvest cards (shown on the card). Harvest cards still roll their own dice when you draw them; the draw is your action.
**Undo.** The last action of a turn can be undone.

**At a table** an **investment** is first **planned**: its project opens in Grow with the numbers, nothing is bought. You decide there how many units to buy and book it with the **buy** button, or you leave it - then the chance is missed with the end of your turn. Everything another player draws and decides is told to the whole table, with the card, and the history lines open the card.
Dice rules at a glance

items: **Every die is yours to throw.** The golden dice on a card is a button; before you throw, the card shows what each number does (green good, red bad, grey nothing).
The **move** is one or two dice (some cards say which). Passing a Payday tile pays; landing on a tile opens its card.
Harvest cards roll their own dice the moment they are drawn; the draw is your action, the dice are shown on the card.
**Undo** takes back the last action of your turn.

blocks.text: You are offered one to three cards (a setting; the default is two). **Every card is one of four kinds**, marked by a coloured badge:

items: **Share** - units with a price; you choose how many to buy, with no limit from the card.
**Investment** - a property or a loan with a deposit, a mortgage and a monthly cash flow.
**Asset** - everything else: a business, a hustle, a coin, a collection.
**Saving** - a free card that lowers one of your expenses.

blocks.text: Each card also carries **keywords** (its market and its group: World stocks, Business, Property, Vending...). The Harvest cards use the same words, so you can see at once whether a market card is about something you own.

**Plan this card.** Taking a card means **planning** it: a Grow project is made with everything the card says, and a note shows how much you have in cash and how much you would have to borrow. You are taken to Grow; a share opens in edit mode so you can set the units. When you press **Buy** the Add dialog books it. **Decline the offer** puts the cards back.

**A card is only buyable while it is in hand.** If you plan a card and do not buy it, the offer is gone when the turn ends - the project closes with a note "Chance missed". A setting (Turns a planned card can be bought, 1 to 3, default 1) gives you more turns.

**Savings cards** cost nothing: they lower the matching expense line (electricity, mobile plan, bank fees...). The Grow project counts **what you have saved so far**, so later you can tell what the saving bought you.
**Side hustles** take your evenings: only three can run at once (a setting); a fourth replaces one.

**Dice cards.** Many cards say "a die decides": a hustle that grows or does not, a business with a good or bad opening, a collection that is worth much or little. The card lists every number; you throw the die after you have bought.

**Traps.** Some offers look like normal investments and are not (a "2% a week" lending app, a "pre-IPO" tip, a timeshare). Their numbers are not given away. The Harvest cards later show which were scams.

**Pensions and employer benefits (S37-S39, P33, T32).** Plans you pay into: you take the card for the length you want (an employer savings plan of 12 Paydays, a company pension of 12 or 24, a state-subsidised pension of 24, a private pension of 36), it becomes a Grow project, and at every Payday the payment goes into it from the **Fire** account (it is money put aside, not an expense). At the end you get back what you paid in **plus a bonus** (50%, 20%, 45%, 35%, 55%: the employer's share, the state's allowance). Stopped early, only what you paid in comes back, less a tenth, and no bonus. The Grow project says how much has gone in so far.

**Career and education (S40, P34, P35, T31).** A course, an evening diploma, a master craftsman's diploma, a part-time master's degree: you pay the fees now, the new pay starts when you have finished (3, 6, 12 or 24 Paydays), and **a die decides how much it raises your income** - nothing, a fair rise, or a big one. Nobody buys a course from you.
What an Opportunity card looks like

Four real cards, one of each kind you meet. The coloured bar is the pile (purple Seed, green Sapling, dark green Tree); the small word is the **kind** - Saving, Share, Asset or Investment. Below the story are the numbers that matter before you buy.

blocks.caption: Examples for looking at - the numbers are those of Jonas (price level 1.0) on Normal. In the game the card also carries its risk, tasks and links in its Grow project.

items.text: You let an AI scan your bank statements. It finds three subscriptions you forgot you had.
items.note: A die decides how much you find: 1-2 gives 15, 3-4 gives 30, 5-6 gives 50 DT a month. Free, and it lasts.

items.title: World ETF Savings Plan
items.text: Fifty euros a month into the whole world economy. Boring. Exactly the point.
items.note: You choose how many units to buy. The price moves with its market index (the Harvest cards move it); you can sell only when a window is open - or at the standing price less 5%.

items.text: 'SQL for Marketing People' - 40 videos recorded over three months.

items.text: Two rooms, sea view, booked solid in summer and empty in February.
items.note: A property with a mortgage: the rent comes in and the mortgage payment goes out every month, so the card shows the cash flow that is left. Several Harvest cards can cut the rent.

blocks.text: In your books
A card you take becomes a **Grow project**. Two examples in the grid of the **Grow** page - **click a card** to open the real info panel (read only): its description, strategy, risk, tasks and notes.

blocks.caption: Example projects in the Grow page. Click one to open the real info panel - for looking only, nothing is saved.

blocks.title: How to read a card in five seconds
blocks.text: Look at the **cost** (can I pay it from cash without the Bank?), the **monthly cash flow or saving** (what does it add to my month?), the **risk** and the **die** (what can it be at worst?). A card that promises a lot for very little is the one to doubt.
Which pile when?

head: Situation
Pile
Why
rows: Free saving cards, a hustle for a few hundred, a first share.
A reserve and a first income
Businesses, bigger shares and hustles; the best pile of the simulation.
Rented flats, shops, franchises; a mortgage is part of the deal.

blocks.title: The card shows its own answers
blocks.text: Every Opportunity card in Grow carries **how to invest**, **what to do**, **what not to do**, its **risk** from 1 to 5 with the reason, tasks and checked links. Read the risk text before you buy: a scam looks like a normal card, and only the numbers give it away.

harvest.title: 🌾 Harvest: the markets
harvest.intro: The market moves, every Harvest card says how, and it tells you if it touches something **you own**.

blocks.text: Every market has an **index** that starts at 1.00 and drifts at every Payday (World stocks, Bonds, Tech, Gold, Bitcoin, Property...). What you own is worth its card price times the index of its market.
A Harvest card can:

items: **move indices** (a crash, a boom) - the value of what you own follows;
open a **window to sell** in a market: only then can you sell shares and coins there;
bring a **buyer** for a property, a business or a collection, at a price that depends on a die;
start a **hype ladder**: stay in while the die wins, cash out before it collapses;
**change the cash flow** of businesses or properties, pause payouts, cut rents, add repairs;
**reveal a scam** and show what was really behind the offer;
change **everyone's costs** for good (inflation) or for some Paydays.

blocks.text: Each card shows its **group** (market, shares, crypto, hype, metals, collectibles, property, business, lending, scam), the **words** it is about - red when you own something with that word -, an **"Affects you / Not about you"** badge, what it does to everybody, and what it means for you. Every affected Grow project gets a note and a highlight.

**Selling what the cards gave you.** What the Opportunity cards made is sold at the price of a Harvest card: in an open market, to a buyer, or on a hype. The offer **stays open for as many of your own turns as the table allows** (the setting How long a sell offer stays open, 1 to 5 turns, 2 by default) even after you pressed **Done** and across a Payday; then the deal is off. While it is open the project in Grow is highlighted and says what it pays and how many turns are left, and its **Sell** button sells at that price.

**Who buys what.** Every kind of holding has buyers among the Harvest cards - about one card in ten speaks of a property, a business, a side hustle, a loan, a collection, a metal or the shares of a market. The price is a roll of the die: a young family pays a little under or a little over what the flat is worth, an institution pays 1% to 20% over the screen price for a block of shares, a search fund pays three years of the profit of a business (at least a share of what you paid), a takeover bid pays a premium. A year-end rally opens every market; a wave of forced selling opens it too - at a loss, so you can also cut it.

**A scam has a last exit.** One card says the price of a scam has fallen by 80% and the market is still open for one more turn; a claims buyer pays cents on the euro; a later card closes it for good. What you do with the last chance is yours.

**Tax on the profit.** A table setting (Tax on the profit of a sale, advanced rules): when you sell something for more than you paid, you owe a share of the **profit** - the default is 26.375%, the German flat tax with the solidarity surcharge; 0 switches it off. The profit is what the sale brings after its costs and what is owed on it (a mortgage), less what you paid for the part you sell. A sale at a loss pays nothing, and the Grow project notes the tax. Pensions pay out untaxed.

**There is always a way out.** A market card with a window or a buyer is the best exit, but it does not come on every landing. So the **Sell** button of a project also sells **at any time at the market price, less a discount**: 5% for a share, 15% for a coin, a collection or a property (the mortgage comes off the proceeds), and a business or a hustle for a year of what it pays (half of what a buyer on a card pays). Nothing is sold below that, and savings and scams cannot be sold at all.
Each Opportunity card has, in its Grow project, how to invest, what to do and what not to do, its risk (1 to 5) with the reason, tasks, and links to read more.

Something breaks. Cards come in five tiers - **spark, flame, blaze, wildfire, inferno** - from a broken bike grip to a house fire. An insurance may cover the bill; the rest is paid from your cash, by a payment plan, or by the Bank loan. In the guided and strict modes an emergency has to be dealt with before the game goes on.

At a **table** the emergency plays as it does alone: you can **pay it now**, spread it over **3, 6 or 12 Paydays** (with the plan's surcharge), or **create the Fire project** - nothing is paid yet, the project opens on the Fire page and you put money into it from there, step by step. In the guided and the strict game the turn is not over before an emergency taken as a Fire project is paid or planned. A fine or a fee that has to be paid at once cannot become a project.
What an Emergency is

Something breaks or goes wrong, and money has to be found. The 50 cards come in five **tiers** - **spark** (a bike grip), **flame**, **blaze**, **wildfire** and **inferno** (the flat burns down) - and in a few **kinds**: a fixed bill, a die that decides the bill, a card with a choice (repair or replace), or a card made of several parts. Some cards need a life you have (a car, a pet, children, a flat of your own); a card for something you do not have is told, put back, and another is drawn.
Who pays first

items.title: Insurance
items.text: If an insurance you hold covers the card, you pay only the **deductible** - at most 500 DT on Normal (300 on Easy, 750 on Hard).

items.title: Your cash
items.text: What is left is paid from your **cash**.

items.title: Your reserve
items.text: If the cash is not enough, the **Mojo** - your emergency reserve - pays the rest. This is what it is for.

items.title: The Bank
items.text: Only when cash and reserve are empty does the **Bank** lend what is missing, in steps of 1,000 DT, at 10% a month.

blocks.text: Three ways to pay

head: Way
What happens
When to use it
rows: The whole bill leaves your cash today.
When your cash and reserve can carry it. The only way for a fine or a fee that must be paid at once.
The bill is split in equal parts, one at every Payday, with a **surcharge**: on Normal 10%, 20% or 35% (Easy 5/10/20, Hard 15/30/50).
When the cash would run dry and you would rather not borrow. It costs less than the Bank (10% **a month**) for a plan up to 12 Paydays.
Nothing is paid yet. The emergency opens as a project on the Fire page and you put money into it from there, step by step.
When you want to pay it with money that comes in over the next turns. In the guided and strict rules the turn is not over until it is paid or planned.

blocks.text: How it looks in the books

An emergency that is not paid at once lives as a **Fire project**: its parts (what the bill is made of), what is paid, the plan and the notes of every payment. Below are two real emergencies in the grid of the **Fire** page: one is paid by a plan of 6 Paydays (the plan is active), one is still planned. **Click a card**: the real info panel of the app opens, read only - the buckets, the payment plan, the tasks and the notes, exactly as in the game.

blocks.caption: Example projects in the Fire page. Click one to open the real info panel - for looking only, nothing is saved.

blocks.title: Why the reserve is the first goal
blocks.text: In the example the player held no disability insurance and the reserve was empty, so the bill had to be spread. With a full reserve (three months of costs) the same card is paid on the spot and forgotten.
Love, a baby, moving in together, a new job, a bad flatmate, a parent who needs help, lifestyle creep. There are four kinds:

items: **Fate** - it happens (you only press Let it happen).
**Choice** - you accept or decline (if the rules allow declining).
**Dice** - a die decides (the baby card: a 1-2 means a baby is on its way in three Paydays).
**Giving** - give, lend, or pass.

blocks.text: Life leaves **lines** behind: a monthly cost that runs for a number of Paydays (a parent who needs help: 6) or for good (lifestyle creep).

Your character climbs a ladder. Jonas starts as a Dual Student (net 1,955 TT a month) and can reach Junior Data Analyst, Data Engineer, Senior Data Engineer, and then split into the technical path (Staff Data Engineer, Chief Data Architect) or the management path (Data Team Lead, Head of Data, Director of Data). A promotion needs a minimum number of Paydays and a successful roll. A promotion raises your salary - and your living costs.
The career of Jonas: the first four stages

Every character has a ladder of their own. This is the beginning of Jonas's: he starts as a **dual student** and climbs to a **senior data engineer** - the pay in the example is his net a month on Normal.

stages.title: Dual Student
stages.story: Three days at the company, two at university. A real salary while you study - and a thesis waiting at the end.
stages.next: To stage 2: at least 3 Paydays, then roll 4 or more. A failed roll (1-2) costs an exam retake of 150 DT.

stages.title: Junior Data Analyst
stages.story: Your bachelor thesis got a 1.3, and your team wants to keep you. First full-time contract!
stages.next: To stage 3: at least 4 Paydays, then roll 4 or more.

stages.title: Data Engineer
stages.story: You automated half the team's reports. Your manager offers you the move into data engineering.
stages.next: To stage 4: at least 4 Paydays, then roll 5 or more.

stages.title: Senior Data Engineer
stages.story: You own the data platform, review everyone's code and mentor two juniors. Five years in, you're senior.
stages.next: To stage 5: at least 5 Paydays, then roll 5 or more - and choose the technical or the management path.

blocks.title: A raise is not all profit
blocks.text: Every step raises your **living costs** too, so the reserve target grows with it (three months of the new costs). Climb when you can, but look at what is left of the month, not at the salary.

Dreams are cards worth **points**, in tiers from little to legendary, in categories like travel, adventure, vehicles, home, learning, creating and giving. Taking a dream makes a **Dream project** with buckets you fill by payment plans. You can have a few open at once. **Dream moments** (an early-bird offer, a gift from family, a last-minute deal, a travel buddy, inspiration, side-project money, points for patience, a dream swap) help a dream along.
What a dream is

Your character has one **life dream** from the start (Jonas: a certified mountain guide). It is the first Dream project and the dream goal of the game. Besides it, the Dream tiles offer **dream cards**: small and big wishes you can add to your Dream page - **48 cards** in tiers from **little** to **legendary**, in categories like travel, adventure, vehicles, home, learning, creating and giving. Every dream card is worth **points**; the bigger the dream, the more points and the higher the price.
How a dream is paid

items.title: You take it
items.text: On a Dream tile you are offered cards. You can take one (it becomes a Dream project), pass, or - where the table allows it - decline all. On Normal you are offered 2 cards, and up to 3 dreams can be open at once.

items.title: It is made of buckets
items.text: Every dream has **buckets**: the journey, the hotel, the equipment, the course. Each has a price and a note of what it is for. You fill them one by one.

items.title: You pay by plan
items.text: A **payment plan** moves a fixed amount into the dream at every Payday - for the example below, 50 DT. You may also put in a lump sum at any time. The plan never forces you; it shows what is due.

items.title: It is lived
items.text: When every bucket is full, the dream is **lived**: it pays out its points and the project closes. For the life dream this ticks the dream goal of the game.

blocks.text: Dream moments

Some Dream tiles bring a **moment** instead of cards: an early-bird offer, a gift from the family, a last-minute deal, a travel buddy, a stroke of inspiration, money from a side project, points for patience, or a swap of one dream for another. They make a dream cheaper or closer - the project notes say by how much.
A dream in the books
Two real dreams in the grid of the **Dream** page: a small one with a plan of 50 a month, and the life dream of Jonas. **Click a card** to open the real info panel (read only).

blocks.caption: Example projects in the Dream page. Click one to open the real info panel - for looking only, nothing is saved.

blocks.title: Dreams and the order of a game
blocks.text: Dreams are the reason to play, but the simulation shows that a player who funds the dream before any income rarely wins. Take the small dreams for the points when a plan of 50 a month does not hurt; keep the big money for cards that pay every month.

notes.title: The notes of a project and what is running

blocks.text: Whatever happens to a Grow, Fire or Dream project is written into its **notes**, with the numbers: what a payment cost, how much cash you had and how much the Bank lent you for it; what a buyer offers (the price, the costs of the sale, what is still owed, what you would receive) or what a market window pays per unit; every step of a hype with the die rolled and what the stake is worth; a sale with what was paid out and the cash afterwards; a dream moment with the cost before and after and what you have saved so far.

A strip above the map shows **every effect that is working on your money right now** and **how many Paydays are left**: costs that run for a while, gains, pauses ("pays nothing for 2 Paydays"), money that is locked, a job search, effects that are on their way and what has changed for good. The character's info lists them in full. When an effect ends, the Payday says so and the project's notes record it - so cash flow never comes back "by magic".

selling.title: Selling: three exits and a tax
selling.intro: Everything you own can be sold except savings, plans and courses. There are three ways, best first - and a tax on the profit that you should count before you press Sell.

head: Exit
Price
When
rows: An open market: every share or coin of that market at its price. A buyer: a die decides (a property 0.85-1.3 times its value, a business 24-36 months of its profit, a block of shares +1% to +20%). A hype: ride it or cash out.
The offer stays open for the table's number of **your own turns** (default 2), even after Done and across a Payday.
The market price less a discount: 5% for a share, 15% for a coin, a collection or a property (the mortgage is paid from the proceeds), a year of the profit for a business or a hustle.
Any time. Use it when you must have cash.
You offer a card in hand to the table; the first to take it gets it.

blocks.text: Selling to step up

The strongest move of the bots is **sell, step up, repeat**: sell a card that has gained and now pays little for what it is worth, and put the money into a bigger card. A small salary reaches a four-figure passive income this way. Count the tax first.
Selling to clear a loan
A Bank loan costs 10% a month. Selling the card that pays least and repaying the loan at once is nearly always better than waiting.
Tax on the profit

A table setting (default **26.375%**, the German flat tax with the solidarity surcharge; `0` switches it off) takes a share of the **profit** of a sale: what the sale brings after its costs and what is owed on it, less what you paid for the part you sell. A sale at a loss pays nothing; pensions pay out untaxed. The Grow project notes the tax.

blocks.title: Scams have a last exit
blocks.text: One card says the price of a scam has fallen by 80% while the market stays open one more turn; a claims buyer pays cents on the euro. What you do with the last chance is yours - and a later card closes it for good.

tables.title: Tables: opening, joining and playing with others
tables.intro: A Dreamer table is a game with two to eight seats, people and bots in any mix.

blocks.text: Finding a table

items: **Open tables** lists public tables with who sits there (picture and rating; tap a face for their profile) and filters: language, ranked or friendly, with or without a clock, characters, how the game ends.
**My tables** are the tables you sit at; **Finished tables** are the last ones you played.
**Join with a code** opens a private table: the host gives you an invite code.

blocks.text: The settings of a new table

head: Setting
What it does
rows: Shown in the lobby. Leave it empty and a funny one is chosen.
How many seats (bots take a seat too).
Everybody, or only people with the invite code.
Easy, Normal or Hard: the numbers of the characters and the cards (see "The characters"). The difficulty is also the stake of the rating.
The result counts for the leaderboard. A ranked table is played under the strict rules, the same for everybody.
Guided: one random card per tile, buying only with the card in hand. Strict: dice only from the app, no free transactions.
Free (the same one twice is fine), unique, or dealt by the table.
**First escape** (the first to reach every goal wins), **all escape** (everybody plays until out or bankrupt) or **after rounds**.
How many points the table asks for, 0 to 60 (0 turns the goal off).
None, per move or a time bank for the whole game. Time out and your turn is played passively.
Fast, normal or slow: how long the bots wait between moves.
People who are not seated may watch.
Dream Taler or a real sign (the numbers do not change).
Tax on the profit of a sale, how long a sell offer stays open (1-5 turns), how many turns a planned card stays buyable (1-3), the Bank loan's interest, undo by vote, leaving, repaying off turn.

blocks.text: The waiting room

The host sees every seat: a person, a bot (with its strategy and level) or empty. The host can add and remove bots, kick a player, change the settings until the game starts and press **Start**. Everybody picks a character and reads the briefing; the game starts when all are ready.
Playing: the queue, the clock and what you see of the others

items: The **queue of players** shows who is on the move, the clock, and who the table waits for.
Everything another player draws and decides is told to the table, with the card. A history line opens the card.
You can look at another player's books (read only) at any time.
If you do not move in time, or lose the connection, your turn is played **passively**. Two missed turns in a row (a setting) mark you **away**; press **I'm back** to return.
**Autoplay while I am away** lets a bot of your strategy play your turns while you are gone. Switch it off in the table menu.
The host may **pause** the game and **close** the table.

blocks.text: Trading cards

Any holding in hand can be offered to the table at a price. The offer panel shows the other players the card, the price per share, the down payment, the mortgage, the cash flow and what it would do to **their** cash and monthly cash flow. They can **buy at the price**, **make a counter offer**, **decline** or **look later**. The first to take it gets it. You can withdraw your offer and accept a counter offer.
Leaving and ending

items: A table with a game that has begun that you **leave** counts as a loss against everybody who stayed (a few free rounds can be set).
A game ends when somebody wins (in first-escape tables), when everybody is done, after the set rounds, or when everybody left.
The end screen shows the trophy, the ranking, the goals ticked and what the game did to your rating.

blocks.text: The game's rules are chosen at the start and cannot change during it:

head: Mode
What it means
rows: Everything is allowed: open any card, sell any time, add any transaction.
One random card per tile, buying only with the card in hand, selling only while a market card offers a buyer (for 3 rolls).
One card per tile, dice only from the app, no free transactions; made for playing with others.

blocks.text: Settings worth knowing: cards offered per Opportunity landing (1-3), side hustles at once (1-5), copies of each savings card (1-3), turns a planned card stays buyable (1-3), the interest of the Bank loan, whether a dream or a life choice may be declined, whether a promotion has to be rolled for.

**Your own settings.** The **Settings** row of the game menu has switches that only you see, kept in your browser: **Notifications** (the small confirmations that pop up; errors always show) and **Messages on the map** (the Payday that just passed, market notices). Turn the notifications off on a phone if they cover buttons.
**The independence badge** compares the passive income with the **cost of living**: the expenses without the income tax and social insurance that stop with the salary. The badge says both numbers.

Every player has **one rating** - the same idea as a chess rating. **Everybody starts at 1500.** It is the middle: the bots on the leaderboard run from about 1270 up to about 1700, so to get to place 1 you play your way up past the best bots. People and bots are on **one list**.
Which games count

A game counts for your rating when the table is **ranked**, at least one person sat at it, the game was **finished**, and it either had a winner or ran **at least 8 rounds**. A game that does not count says why at the end ("Not ranked: under 8 rounds"). If you leave a game that has begun, it counts as a loss against everybody who stayed.
How a game places everybody
At the end every player gets a score:

head: What
Points
rows: Each goal, in proportion to how far you got (the reserve, no debts, the dream, independence): a goal reached is 250, one that is 60% done is 150

blocks.text: The order: whoever won comes first (the earliest winner on top), then everybody by score, and a tie is decided by net worth. A player who went bankrupt, or left, is behind everybody who did not.
From the place to your points
Your place is compared with **each other player at the table**, one by one. Placing above a player is a win against them, below is a loss.

items: Beating a player with a **higher** rating earns **more** than beating one with a lower rating.
Losing to a player with a **lower** rating costs **more** than losing to a higher one.
The bigger the gap, the more surprising the result - and the more it moves you.

blocks.text: You gain or lose the average of these duels. As a feeling: at a table of four players with equal ratings, **first place is about +20** and **last place about -13** (in your first 20 games the numbers are bigger, so a new rating finds its place quickly; they are shown with a `~` until you have played 5 games). Winning against three bots rated 1700 is worth about +30, against three bots rated 1300 about +10.
Harder game, more points
The difficulty of the game is the **stake**: the points you **gain** are multiplied.

So the same win at an even table is about +14 on Easy, +20 on Normal and +30 on Hard. A bad game costs the same everywhere - so you never lose more for daring Hard. The character matters too: some characters are harder than others (we know it from thousands of simulated games), so the same place earns a little more with a hard character and a little less with an easy one.
The bots

Every bot is a **strategy** at a **skill level** (master, strong, casual, beginner) - the master plays its strategy cleanly, the others slip now and then. Each has its own rating from the start, set by a tournament the bots played against each other, and it moves with its games like yours. That is why a beginner bot sits low and the best masters near 1700.
The leaderboard
One list, best rating first. A person is on it only after switching on **Show me on the leaderboard**; a bot appears once it has played a ranked game. The rating never falls below 100.

profile.title: The profile of a player and the fact table
profile.intro: Every person and every bot on the leaderboard has a profile. Tap a name to open it.

items.title: The rating line
items.text: How the rating moved: **from 1500** (or the bot's base rating) over every ranked game, with the place and the change of each game.

items.title: The counters
items.text: Games, table wins, average place, goals reached, bankruptcies, best rating.

items.title: The fact table
items.text: What the games came to in the four places of the method, as a **total** and an **average per game**.

head: Place
What it counts
rows: Cards bought and sold, holdings at the end, share lots, properties, businesses and hustles, pension plans, courses and degrees, money put into cards.
Whether the reserve was full and how much it was, debts repaid and left, the Bank loan, emergencies paid and what they cost.
Life dream lived, dreams lived and their money, dreams still open, money saved for dreams, dream points.
Independent or not, passive income, salary, cash flow, living costs, what the cards earned, net worth.
blocks.note: Games played before the fact table existed have none and are not counted in it.

blocks.title: Use it
blocks.text: Open the profile of the best bot and compare its fact table with yours: it shows what a winning life looks like - how many cards, how early a full reserve, how much the cards earned.

bots.title: The bots: who they are and how they were made
bots.intro: The bots are not scripted. Each one is a **strategy** at a **skill level**, its numbers were found by simulation, and it is rated like a person.

blocks.text: Strategies

head: Strategy
In one line
rows: Reserve first, then cards that pay every month, sells into good windows. The best all-rounder.
Lives on businesses and hustles from the middle pile; never property. The champion of the champions of the first calibration.
Free savings first, then only Trees. Slow but strong at the top of the tournament.
A world ETF and bonds for the steady part.
Dividend shares from all piles, reinvested.
One side hustle after the other, reinvesting every month.
Three months of cash, no risky card.
Puts the dream and its points first.
Savings and the employer's money; few risks.
Crypto, hype and hot tips. Almost never wins, but it makes the table lively.

blocks.text: Skill levels

The same strategy at four levels: **master** (plays it cleanly), **strong** (slips 10% of the decisions), **casual** (25%) and **beginner** (45%). A bot is called `strategy` or `strategy--level`. A beginner sits low on the leaderboard, a master near the top.
Everything the bots can do

The bots know **every capability of the game**: choosing a pile and a card, planning and buying, taking free savings and pensions, courses, funding the reserve and dreams, payment plans, insurances, repaying debts and the Bank loan, selling into market windows, to buyers and on hypes, riding or cashing out a hype, selling to step up, selling to clear a loan, trading with other players, and emergencies and life cards. One capability, **planning a purchase for later**, no bot uses yet.
How the strategies were found

items.title: Capabilities
items.text: A list of everything a player can do is checked by a test: a new move cannot be forgotten.

items.title: Relearn
items.text: For every strategy a search moves one to three knobs at a time (how much cash to keep, how fast to plan, how much to risk, when to sell ...) and plays thousands of solo games on random characters, difficulties and maps. A change is kept only when it is better **by a clear margin on fresh games**, so a run that finds nothing leaves everything as it was.

items.title: Tournament
items.text: All bots, every strategy at every level, play thousands of tables of four against each other on each difficulty and are rated with the same Elo as the leaderboard. A new bot starts at 1500 and travels to its place.

items.title: Gauntlet
items.text: The six best masters meet again on fresh seeds; the one that wins most tables is the **champion of the champions**.

blocks.title: The first full calibration (2026-11-06)
blocks.text: 183 minutes; 13 of 14 strategies found a stronger version (ETF 27% to 66% wins, Tree 22% to 50%, Dreamer 32% to 57%, Saver 7% to 31%). On the tables the top was Tree, Sapling and Expert; **Sapling** is the champion of the champions with 33% of the gauntlet tables. The numbers are in the last section.

strategy.title: Strategy: how the game is won
strategy.intro: The knowledge of the simulation, in the order a game goes.

items.title: The first months: free money and a reserve
items.text: Take the **Seed saving cards** (a cheaper phone plan, electricity, a job ticket, an audit of subscriptions): they cost nothing and lift the month. Take the employer's savings plan and a company pension when the month can carry them. Put free money into the **reserve** until it covers three months.

items.title: A first income
items.text: A side hustle or a small business (Seed and Sapling), a world ETF or dividend shares, a room rented out. Only a few side hustles can run at a time. A card that pays every month beats one that only might rise.

items.title: The debts
items.text: Repay the starting debts when the cash allows; a debt with interest first.

items.title: Step up
items.text: Sell a card at a good price and buy a bigger one from the Sapling or Tree pile. **Sell, step up, repeat.**

items.title: Raise the pay
items.text: A course or a diploma costs now and raises the pay after a few Paydays by a die. Worth it early; keep the reserve.

items.title: The dream
items.text: Fund it with what is left, with a plan per Payday. Take dreams for the points only when the income carries part of it.

items.title: Take
items.text: Free savings, employer and state benefits, ETFs and dividend funds for the steady part, businesses and properties whose cash flow covers their loan, anything with a payment you can check.

items.title: Leave
items.text: A **fixed high return** (a weekly interest), a **hot tip**, a **pre-IPO** share, a **timeshare**, a **trading-signals course**, a coin nobody knows. They look like any card but are scams; the more it promises for how little, the less true it is.

items.title: Be careful with
items.text: Crypto, collectibles and hype (they swing and pay nothing monthly), and a Tree card bought with a Bank loan.

items.title: Never
items.text: Keep a Bank loan open when the cash could repay it.

blocks.text: The simulation (below) has tried twelve ways of playing. They are ideas to steal:

items: **The informed investor** takes every free saving, then whatever pays most for its price from all three piles, funds the reserve and the dream by payment plans, and starts the dream only when the passive income helps carry it.
**The Sapling builder** lives on businesses and hustles from the middle pile and never buys property.
**The hustler** starts one side hustle after the other and reinvests every month.
**The dividend snowball** collects dividend shares of all piles and reinvests.
**The Tree saver** takes only free savings until a Tree is affordable, then buys only Trees.
**The steady builder** keeps three months of cash and takes no risky card.

blocks.text: What does not work: living on free cards only, speculating on crypto and hot tips, and putting the dream before everything.

blocks.title: Judge in the light of the character
blocks.text: A surgeon on Hard wins about 3 in 100 simulated games; a bus driver on Easy over 80. A score is not comparable across characters, a **pace** is. See "The characters".

items.term: I am stuck. What should I do now?
items.text: Look at the goals: the lowest bar is your task. Without a reserve, fund the reserve. Without income, take free savings and a first hustle. Then ask for the **demo game** or an agent for advice.

items.term: Why did the card say "lucky" and draw another?
items.text: The card needed something your life does not have (a car, a child, a partner). It is told, put back, and the next one is drawn.

items.term: Why can I not sell this?
items.text: Savings, plans and courses cannot be sold. A scam can be sold only at the last exit its card gives. Everything else sells at any time at the standing price.

items.term: I planned a card and lost it.
items.text: A planned card is only buyable while it is in hand: the offer is gone when your turn ends (a setting allows up to 3 turns). The project closes with a note "Chance missed".
A negative monthly cash flow means **bankruptcy**: the game ends for you. Watch the money panel before a card that adds a cost.

items.term: Why did my rating not change?
items.text: The game was not ranked, had no person at the table, ended before 8 rounds without a winner, or was not finished. The end screen says why.

blocks.text: What the simulation found, and what we changed
Read the tables with care: with 200 games per way of playing, differences of a few points are noise. Only big gaps mean something.

items: **The Sapling pile was too strong.** In a first play a Sapling business with 8,000 TT of capital paid up to 3,900 TT a month on a six - more than the whole salary, in the seventh month of the game. Since then a Sapling business pays **40%** of what the sketch said: the best single Sapling card now pays about 1,500 TT a month on a six and 300-650 on average. Three thousand a month is only possible with a Tree.

**The Sapling pile is still the engine of the game.** The ten cards with the biggest gap in the win chance are all Sapling cards (E-Bike Rental Fleet, Laundry Pick-Up, Rent Out a Room, Snack Vending Machine, Freelance Data Consulting...): a player who owns one of them wins about half of the games, one who owns none wins about one in ten. That is meant - a good start is what a promotion buys - but none of them may become much better.

**The Trees are out of reach for Jonas.** Almost nobody buys a Tree: a flat needs 11,000 TT of cash and Jonas saves 300-450 TT a month. The "Tree saver" wins 1% of its games. Trees are the late game of a character with a better salary, or of a player who has a few Saplings running. If the Trees should matter earlier, the cheapest Tree (a studio flat) or the Tree pile's cost is the knob.

**The free savings cards are a pillar.** Every won game took all six free savings cards (the electricity provider, the mobile plan, the free bank account, the job ticket, the AI subscription audit, the contract check): together they are worth 40-50 TT a month for nothing, and a player without them hardly ever wins. They are also the reason "Free cards only" does not win: they are the start, not the way.

**Four ways of playing work**: the informed investor (44%), the Sapling builder (40%), the steady builder (17%) and the side hustler (17%). The wins come about month 51-54 (a normal game is about 36 months, so Medium is still too hard on average; the quickest win was month 38).

**Four ways of playing do not work, as intended**: living on free cards only, the gambler, the dream chaser and the tree saver win almost never. The gambler and the free-cards player are also the only ones who go bankrupt now and then.
**Dream before everything loses.** The dream chaser reaches the dream first (month 48) but never builds income.

**Events.** No Emergency or Life card breaks the game by itself. The ones that cost most are the monthly lines: Family in Need, Grandpa's Old Car, Lifestyle Creep, a baby. A player who meets them early wins less often, but never by more than a few points. In the market cards Hype Fades, Exchange Collapse and Inflation Spike are the worst; Major Repair and Collector Hype help a lot, which says more about who owns property and collectibles than about the card.

**The first human game was far faster than any bot** (financial independence in month 7, against month 38 for the quickest bot). It needed a promotion, a 6 on a business die and a lucky purchase; the changes above take that path away. The next play will tell whether Medium is now too hard or right.
